title: The first screen of a billing tool
metaTitle: The first screen of a billing tool
excerpt: A finance lead afraid of a wrong invoice needs the next invoice and one action. The first screen should name that object, not start a tour.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, a small group paused before the next decision.
caption: Three cups over a wooden table, a pause before the next move. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a billing tool show?
faqs.answer: Show the next invoice that needs a human, and one action. For a finance lead afraid of a wrong invoice, that usually means the draft about to send, or the charge that failed, with the amount, the recipient, and the status in the first glance. A tour of charts is not that object.

faqs.question: Are revenue charts a bad first screen?
faqs.answer: They are the wrong first screen for the person whose fear is sending the wrong invoice. Charts answer how the month is going. The first screen should answer which invoice needs a decision before it goes out. Put charts where a review happens, not in front of the send button.

faqs.question: How do we test it?
faqs.answer: Hand the lead a real invoice they are nervous about, or a faithful copy, and see whether they can confirm amount, recipient, and status without opening a second page. If they ask 'has this been sent,' the first screen failed.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Billing tool UX on the first screen should name the next invoice and the one action, not start a tour. The person in front of it is a finance lead who is afraid of a wrong invoice. They are not here to be inspired by revenue. They are here to see the amount, the recipient, and whether the thing has already gone out.

If those three facts are not in the first glance, the screen is hiding the only fear that matters.

## The fear is a wrong send

A wrong invoice is not a usability nit. It is a customer who trusts you less, a ledger that has to be unwound, and a morning spent explaining a number. The first screen should be built around preventing that, the way a cockpit puts the altitude where the eye already is. Decoration around it is not neutral. It is cover.

The object is a specific invoice. "Acme, draft, $4,200, not sent." That is a headline. "Good morning, here is your overview" is a lobby. Lobbies are where anxious people click the wrong card. Put the invoice that is closest to leaving the building at the top. If nothing is close to sending, say that, in a sentence, and show the next thing that does need a human: a failed payment, a draft waiting on tax, a credit that has not been applied. Empty bravado, a confetti state that says all caught up when three drafts sit underneath, is how the fear gets confirmed later.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) gives extra weight, in its notion of trust, to topics that can affect someone's financial stability. An invoice tool is that kind of product even when the audience is a small company rather than a bank. Trust on this screen is not a badge in the footer. It is whether the number on the glass is the number that will be sent. Do not round it into a friendlier figure. Do not abbreviate the customer into a logo you hope they recognize. Spell the name. Show the currency. Show the status in a word you would say out loud: draft, scheduled, sent, paid, void.

## Amount, recipient, status, one verb

Four elements. The amount, large enough to read without leaning in, with the currency code beside it so a dollar and a similarly symbolled currency cannot swap in a hurry. The recipient, legal name and the email it will go to, because the wrong email is a wrong invoice even when the math is right. The status, a word, not a color alone. And one verb that matches the status. "Review and send" for a draft. "Fix payment" for a failure. "Void" is not the verb of the first screen unless they came here to void. A screen with Send, Void, Duplicate, and Remind all in the same weight is a menu of regrets.

The line items that make up the amount should be one tap away and visible enough that the total is not a magic number. A finance lead will not send what they cannot explain. Show the first lines, and a count if there are more. If tax is included, say so in the same glance. "Tax not calculated" is a status, and it should block the send verb rather than sit as a footnote under a live button.

[Nielsen Norman Group's work on how quickly people leave](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is about web pages and the first 10 to 20 seconds. A billing home is a page. In those seconds the lead is doing threat detection, not exploration. If the first thing they see is a chart of the quarter, they have to hunt for the invoice that might be wrong. Some of them will send nothing, which is its own failure. Some will send from a different screen they trust more, such as a PDF they exported last week, and your tool becomes a diary instead of a control. Put the threat, which is the unsent or the failed invoice, in the spot the chart wanted.

## Why a tour is an insult here

A product tour on this screen says you think they are new to the idea of an invoice. They are not. They are new, at most, to your arrangement of it. Teach with labels, not with a spotlight sequence. "This has not been sent" next to the status teaches the only lesson that matters on day one. A five-step coach mark teaches them to click Skip, and then to distrust anything else that pops up, including a real warning.

Charts can exist. They answer a different session, the weekly look at what is outstanding. Give that session a destination. Do not make it the door. A door made of charts trains people to admire the month and miss the draft scheduled for 4 p.m. If something is scheduled, the schedule is the object. "Sends today at 4" is a more important sentence than the growth rate.

Upsells do not belong here either. "Add a payment method," "invite your accountant," "try usage-based pricing" are company goals. The lead's goal is to not be wrong. You may offer an accountant invite inside the cabinet of settings, or when they export. You may not put it above the amount. Every pixel above the amount is a pixel they must decide to ignore, and anxious scanning is how details get skipped.

Also refuse a sample invoice that looks real. Demo data that uses a plausible customer name is a disaster waiting for a screenshot or, worse, a send. If the account is empty, say it is empty. Show a clearly marked example only inside a help surface, with send disabled and the word "example" in the recipient line. The first screen of a live account should never contain fiction.

## Drafts that are about to leave

Sort by danger, not by recency of edit and not by size. A small invoice to the wrong familiar customer is more dangerous than a large draft nobody has scheduled. Danger is: scheduled soon, failed and retrying, sent and disputed, draft with tax incomplete. Label the sort in plain speech. "Needs you before it sends." That phrase is the first screen's title when the list is not a single invoice.

A single invoice can still be the whole screen when one is imminent. Do not show a list of twenty with the urgent one in the same type as the rest. Promote it. The others can be a quiet list below, or a count. "4 other drafts, none scheduled." That count prevents the promoted invoice from hiding the rest without turning the screen back into a table.

The send verb, when they reach it, should restate the facts it will commit. "Send $4,200 to Acme at ap@acme.com." A button that only says "Send" after they have scrolled is how the recipient line scrolls out of mind. Restate it on the button's confirmation, every time, including the second time today. Familiarity is not a reason to shorten the confirmation. Familiarity is when mistakes happen, because the customer name looks like the one they sent yesterday.

Scheduled sends need a clock the lead believes. Show the time zone in words. "Today, 4:00 p.m. Central." A timestamp without a zone is a future argument. Let them stop the schedule from this screen without a hunt through settings. Stopping a wrong send is the action, just as much as sending a right one.

## What a returning lead needs

They were here an hour ago. Show what changed. "Payment failed on the Acme invoice after you left." That line is the opposite of a cheerful empty state. If nothing changed, do not invent a change to seem alive. "No invoices sent since you were here" is a calming fact. Say it.

Restore any half-written memo or internal note. Internal notes are where leads write "do not send until the PO arrives." Losing that note is how the invoice goes anyway. The note is not decoration. It is a control. Put it on the first screen of that invoice, under the amount, in a place that is read before the verb.

If two people might send, show the other person's presence. "Jordan is viewing this draft." Collisions on invoices create double sends and polite panics. You do not need a full collaborative suite. You need one line and a lock on the verb if your product cannot safely merge two sends. Pick a rule and write it: only one person can press send, the other can comment. Then implement the rule. A warning that does not lock is a suggestion. Suggestions get overridden at 4 p.m.

## What stays off this screen

Keep the first screen free of:

1. A product tour, a changelog, and a welcome.
2. Revenue charts and goal thermometers.
3. Plan upsells and integration marketplaces.
4. Settings for tax rates and payment processors.
5. Any sample data that could be mistaken for a customer.

The lead can reach settings when they mean to change a rate. They should not trip over it on the way to a status. Search belongs at the edge, for the moment the invoice you surfaced is not the one they fear. The edge is not the center. The center is the amount and the verb.

Brand, on this screen, is accuracy and calm type. Hanabi's interface work, visible in products like Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai, is the standard to borrow: one hierarchy, nothing extra in the scan path. A billing tool can be beautiful. Beauty here is the number being impossible to misread. It is not a texture behind the total.

## Defend it with one invoice

In review, open the screen with one real-shaped invoice and cover the rest with your hand. Can you still answer: who, how much, what currency, sent or not, and what the button will do? If you need the charts to feel the screen is "complete," the screen is serving the demo. Strip it until the hand test passes. Then add back only what the lead asked for while doing that test.

Ask them, out loud, "would you send this?" If they hesitate, ask what is missing. Add that, and nothing else. Hesitation is the fear doing its job. The product should answer the hesitation, not route around it with a brighter button.

When the verb fails, the next screen is not a chart either. [Errors in a billing tool](/blog/errors-in-a-billing-tool) is the next piece, because a failed send has to say whether the invoice went out and what to do, without a code and a sad drawing.
